procedural_history.originating_court: Tahsildar (first instance), then Deputy Collector (Tenancy Appeals), then Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 1, 1966, of the Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench in Special Civil Application No. 190 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a petition under Art. 227 of the Constitution challenging the order made in the case of respondent No. 1 alone. The Bombay High Court dismissed the petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave after the Bombay High Court dismissed his petition.

directions: there will be no order as to costs

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was entitled to raise a contention based on s. 42(c) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, for the first time before the High Court without any foundation in the pleadings.

facts.fact: The appellant filed an application for possession of land against the tenant (respondent No. 1).
The case went through three lower authorities: the Tahsildar, the Deputy Collector, and the Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal.
The appellant did not refer to or rely on section 42(c) of the Act in the initial application (pleadings) or before any of these three authorities.
The appellant raised the contention based on section 42(c) for the very first time when the matter reached the High Court.

law.law_text: A party is not entitled to raise a new legal contention at a late stage of litigation (such as before the High Court) if no foundation for that contention was laid in the initial pleadings or argued at any prior stage.

application.application_text: The Supreme Court noted that the appellant's original application was not founded on any facts or pleas relevant to section 42(c).
The Court observed that the argument based on section 42(c) was never raised before any of the revenue authorities, including the Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal.

Because the appellant failed to lay any groundwork for this argument in the pleadings or at any earlier stage, the Court determined that the appellant was procedurally barred from introducing it for the first time before the High Court.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the appellant was not entitled to raise an argument based on section 42(c) for the first time before the High Court because no foundation for it had been laid in the pleadings or at any prior stage of the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the tenant (first respondent) had become a statutory owner of the land under s. 46(1) of the Act on April 1, 1961, even without taking steps to purchase the land.

facts: The first respondent was a protected lessee (tenant) of land owned by the appellant (landlord).
The appellant filed for possession of the land, arguing the tenant had failed to exercise his right to purchase it.
The lower authorities, including the tribunal, held that the tenant had become a statutory owner on April 1, 1961, under Section 46(1) of the Act.

law.law_provision: Section 46(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958
law.explanation: This section provided for the automatic transfer of ownership of land to tenants on April 1, 1961, if they were entitled to purchase the land from their landlord.
This was a new sub-section inserted by an amending Act in 1962, which the appellant argued required the tenant to take steps to purchase the land.
A provision (later deleted) that the appellant argued limited the tenant's right to purchase, thereby preventing the transfer of ownership under s. 46(1).

application.reasoning: The Court held that Section 46(1) of the Act operated automatically. By virtue of this provision, the ownership of the land stood transferred to and vested in the tenant on the specified date of April 1, 1961.
evidence: We concur in the view of the tribunal that respondent No. 1 became a statutory owner of the land in his tenancy by virtue of s. 46(1) of the Act with effect from April 1, 1961 even though he did not take steps to purchase that land from the appellant under s. 43.

application.reasoning: The Court rejected the appellant's argument based on the subsequent insertion of Section 43(14A). It reasoned that this amendment, which came into force in 1962, did not have retrospective effect and therefore could not affect the ownership that had already been transferred to the tenant in 1961.
evidence: The operation of s. 46(1) could not be affected by the subsequent insertion of sub-s. (14-A) in s. 43 which did not have retrospective operation.

application.reasoning: The Court refused to consider the appellant's contention based on Section 42(c) on procedural grounds, stating that the appellant had failed to raise this issue in the initial pleadings or at any stage before the case reached the High Court.
evidence: The appellant was not entitled to raise any contention based on s. 42(c) as no foundation was laid for doing so in the plead· ings or at any prior state till the matter reached the High Court.

application.reasoning: The Court also noted that there were no pending proceedings for termination of the tenancy, which was a condition that could have delayed the transfer of ownership under s. 46(1).
evidence: As there was no proceeding pending for termination of the tenancy of respondent No. 1 the conclusion of the tribunal that respondent No. 1 had become a statutory owner on Aprill, 1961 was upheld.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the tenant had become the statutory owner of the land on April 1, 1961, due to the automatic operation of Section 46(1) of the Act. This transfer of ownership occurred by law on that date, even though the tenant had not taken any active steps to purchase the land. The Court dismissed the landlord's counter-arguments, finding that a subsequent, non-retrospective amendment (s. 43(14A)) could not undo the vested ownership, and another argument (based on s. 42(c)) was procedurally barred as it was not raised in a timely manner.

issue.issue_text: Whether the operation of s. 46(1) of the Act was affected by the subsequent insertion of sub-section (14A) in s. 43, which did not have retrospective operation.

facts: Respondent No. 1 was a tenant on land owned by the appellant.
Section 46(1) of the Act provided for the automatic transfer of ownership to tenants on April 1, 1961.
Sub-section (14A) was inserted into Section 43 by an amending Act that came into force on March 1, 1962, almost a year after the date specified in s. 46(1).
The new sub-section (14A) was not given retrospective operation.
law: Under Section 46(1) of the Act, ownership of land automatically transferred to and vested in the tenant on April 1, 1961, making the tenant a statutory owner.
A statutory provision that does not have retrospective operation cannot affect legal rights and events that were already finalized before that provision came into force.
application: The Court, concurring with the tribunal, found that the tenant (respondent No. 1) had already become the statutory owner of the land on April 1, 1961, by the automatic operation of Section 46(1).
This vesting of ownership was a completed event that occurred before sub-section (14A) was added to the Act.
Since sub-section (14A) was inserted subsequently and did not have retrospective effect, it could not undo or alter the transfer of ownership that had already taken place under Section 46(1).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the operation of Section 46(1), which had already made the tenant the statutory owner on April 1, 1961, could not be affected by the later insertion of sub-section (14A) into Section 43, as the new provision was not retrospective.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was entitled to raise a contention based on s. 42(c) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, for the first time before the High Court without any foundation in the pleadings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that under s. 42(c), the landlord was entitled to retain land to the extent of one family holding, and therefore the tenant was not entitled to purchase the entire land, which was a pre-condition for the transfer of ownership under s. 46(1).
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the court, was that this contention could not be raised as it was not referred to or relied upon before any of the revenue authorities and was not founded on any facts or pleas in the original application.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the tenant (first respondent) had become a statutory owner of the land under s. 46(1) of the Act on April 1, 1961, even without taking steps to purchase the land.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that ownership was not transferred to the tenant on April 1, 1961, because the condition in s. 42(c) (that the landlord be left with one family holding) was not fulfilled, and the tenant had failed to exercise his right of purchase.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that he had automatically become the owner of the land on April 1, 1961, by virtue of the provisions of s. 46(1) of the Act, even if he did not apply to purchase the land.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the operation of s. 46(1) of the Act was affected by the subsequent insertion of sub-section (14A) in s. 43, which did not have retrospective operation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that since ownership was not transferred on April 1, 1961, the tenant's right to purchase was governed by the subsequently inserted s. 43(14A). As the tenant failed to exercise his right under this new provision, the land must be deemed to have been surrendered to the landlord.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the lower courts, was that s. 43(14A) was irrelevant because it came into existence after he had already become the owner on April 1, 1961, under s. 46(1). Therefore, no tenancy rights were left to be surrendered under the new provision.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statutory right that has vested in a person is not affected by a subsequent statutory amendment unless that amendment has retrospective operation. Furthermore, a party is not entitled to raise a legal contention at a late appellate stage if no foundation for it was laid in the pleadings or at any prior stage of the proceedings.
obiter: The court's final opinion on the scope and ambit of s. 42(c) was expressly withheld.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concurred with the tribunal's view that the first respondent had become a statutory owner of the land in his tenancy by virtue of s. 46(1) of the Act with effect from April 1, 1961, even though he did not take steps to purchase that land from the appellant. This vested ownership could not be affected by the subsequent insertion of sub-section (14-A) in s. 43, as that amendment did not have retrospective operation.
legal_tests_applied: A party is not entitled to raise a new contention before a higher court if no foundation was laid for it in the pleadings or at any prior stage of the proceedings.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant was not entitled to raise any contention based on s. 42(c) because "no foundation was laid for doing so in the pleadings or at any prior stage except before the High Court."

The appellant's argument regarding the subsequently inserted s. 43(14A) failed because the tenant's ownership had already vested on April 1, 1961, and the new provision "did not have retrospective operation."
why_respondent_won: The respondent became a statutory owner of the land on April 1, 1961, by virtue of s. 46(1) of the Act, even without applying to purchase the land.

The appellant's primary contention regarding s. 42(c) was procedurally barred as it "was neither referred to nor relied upon before any of the revenue authorities" and the original application "was not founded on any facts or pleas relevant to s. 42( c)."
policy_considerations: The court noted that the appellant's contention based on s. 42(c) "leads to unusual and strange results," questioning how the appellant could selectively target one tenant to satisfy the landholding requirement while abandoning similar claims against other tenants.
